A health researcher wants to test whether college students at a local university drink a different amount of water daily compared to the national average. Health guidelines estimate that the national average daily water intake for young adults is 2000 mL.
The researcher selects a simple random sample of \(n = 50\) students from the campus library and records their daily water consumption in milliliters (mL). You want to investigate if students at this particular college are different than the national average. Assume that \(\bar{x}\) = 2035mL, and \(s\) = 150mL.
\(Ho: \mu = 2000\)
\(Ha: \mu \neq 2000\)
What is \(\mu\) in the context of the problem?

title: Review-Part 2
text:
t vs z test
We use a Z-distribution (standard normal) when:
– Working with a categorical response (single proportion test)
– When \(\sigma\) is known (almost never)
We use a t-distribution when:
– Working with a quantitative response (single mean test)

The probability of observing a mean of 2035, or something more extreme, given the population mean of water intake for young adults is 2000 mL, is about 10.53%.
This allows us to write a decision and conclusion about our research study!

title: Review-Part 2
text:
Decisions and conclusions
In fixed level testing, you often set a \(\alpha\) prior to conducting your study.
What is \(\alpha\)?

title: Review-Part 2
text:
α
– significance level
– Type I error rate
– Tool we use to compare our p-value to, and see if we have enough evidence to reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis!

title: Review-Part 2
text:
Type I error rate
Probability that we reject the null hypothesis, given the null hypothesis is actually true!
We don’t know if we make a Type-1 error in practice, but this is the probability that we do!
Typically \(\alpha\) is 0.01, 0.05, or 0.10.
Often depends on the field you work in.
Fisher (famous statistician) suggested that 5% was a convenient cutoff for judging whether results were unusual under the null hypothesis.
\(\alpha\) is often chosen based on the consequences of making an error.

title: Review-Part 2
text:
Decision
\(\alpha\) = 0.05 p-value ~ .1053
We always always always write decisions in the context of the null hypothesis!
\(Ho: \mu = 2000\)
What would be our decision in this context?

title: Review-Part 2
text:
Conclusions
We always always always write conclusions in the context of the alternative hypothesis!
\(Ho: \mu \neq 2000\)
What would our conclusion be?

A health researcher wants to test whether college students at a local university drink a different amount of water daily compared to the national average. Health guidelines estimate that the national average daily water intake for young adults is 2000 mL.
The researcher selects a simple random sample of \(n = 50\) students from the campus library and records their daily water consumption in milliliters (mL). We want to estimate the population mean water consumption for these students on campus. Assume that \(\bar{x}\) = 2035mL, and \(s\) = 150mL

title: Review-Part 2
text:
Confidence Interval
You may use 2.01 for \(t^*\). Calculate a 95% confidence interval using the formula below.
\[\bar{x} \pm t^* \cdot \left( \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} \right)\]

title: Review-Part 2
text:
Confidence Interval
\[\bar{x} \pm t^* \cdot \left( \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} \right)\]
\[2035 \pm 2.010 \cdot \left( \frac{150}{\sqrt{50}} \right)\]
\[2035 \pm 2.010 \cdot (21.2132)\]
\[2035 \pm 42.64\]
\[(1992.36\text{ mL},\ 2077.64\text{ mL})\]
how do we interpret this?

title: Review-Part 2
text:
Interpretation
We are 95% confident that the true mean water consumption of students at this certain university is between \((1992.36\text{ mL},\ 2077.64\text{ mL})\)!
– Note: We are saying confident and not probability!
– Note: All interpretations (including this one) are in the context of the problem!

title: Review-Part 2
text:
Categorical Data
A health researcher wants to see if more than half of college students are drinking water. In a sample size of \(n = 50\), the researcher recorded that 35 students drink more than 1 bottle of water a day.
What’s different than before?
What’s the null and alternative hypothesis?
What type of test are we doing?

title: Review-Part 2
text:
Null and alternative
\(Ho: \pi = .5\)
\(Ha: \pi > .5\)
We are going to conduct a z-test, because our response variable is categorical!

title: Review-Part 2
text:
t vs z-test
\[{SE(\bar{x})} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]
\[\text{Sample Standard Deviation } (s) = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}}\]
\(vs\)
\[{SE(p_o)} = \sqrt{\frac{p_0(1 - p_0)}{n}}\]
Because we know the standard error when we calculate our statistic \(\hat{p}\), we are justified to do a z-test and a standard normal distribution.

title: Review-Part 2
text:
Other formulas
\[z = \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{\frac{p_0(1 - p_0)}{n}}}\]
\[\hat{p} \pm z^* \cdot \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}{n}}\]

title: Review-Part 2
text:
Assumptions
Hypothesis test:
\[n p_0 \ge 10 \quad \text{and} \quad n (1 - p_0) \ge 10\]
Confidence interval:
\[n \hat{p} \ge 10 \quad \text{and} \quad n (1 - \hat{p}) \ge 10\]

title: Review-Part 2
text:
z-statistic
\[z \approx 2.83\]
Draw out how the p-value would be calculated.

title: Review-Part 2
text:
Confidence interval
We are using the z* for a 95% confidence interval!
\[\hat{p} \pm z^* \cdot \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}{n}}\]

title: Review-Part 2
text:
Confidence interval
\[(0.5730,\ 0.8270) \quad \text{or} \quad (57.30\%,\ 82.70\%)\]
How do we interpret this?

title: Review-Part 2
text:
Interpretation
We are 95% confident that the true proportion of students who drink at least one bottle of water a day is between (57.30%, 82.70%).
– Note: We are using the word confident and not probability!
– This (and other) interpretations are in the context of the problem!

title: Review-Part 2
text:
z-scores
A z-score describes an individual observation, while a test statistic is used to test a hypothesis about a population.
Z-score:
\[z = \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\]
T-statistic:
\[t = \frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}}\]

title: Review-Part 2
text:
z-scores
A z-score can answer questions like:
“How unusual is this individual observation compared with the population?”

title: Review-Part 2
text:
Question
Suppose the average wait time at a coffee shop is 5 minutes, with a standard deviation of 1.5 minutes.
You wait 9 minutes.
How unusual is an 8-minute wait compared with the typical wait?

title: Review-Part 2
Review-Part 2
text:
z-scores
We also often calculate z-scores to compare between each other.
Suppose the average wait time at a coffee shop is 5 minutes, with a standard deviation of 1.5 minutes. You wait 9 minutes.
You then go to a second coffee shop. The average wait time at the second coffee shop is 8 mintes, with a standard deviation of 3 minutes. You wait 11.5 minutes. Which is more unlikely?

title: Review-Part 2
text:
Coffee z-scores
Coffee Shop 1
\[
z_1 = \frac{9-5}{1.5}
= \frac{4}{1.5}
\approx 2.67
\]
Coffee Shop 2
\[
z_2 = \frac{11.5-8}{3}
= \frac{3.5}{3}
\approx 1.17
\]
Since \(2.67 > 1.17\), the 9-minute wait at Coffee Shop 1 is more unlikely.

title: ST311 Review
text:
Degrees of freedom
The Wardrobe Analogy
Imagine you have 7 different shirts to wear over a 7-day week. On Monday, you have 7 choices. On Tuesday, 6 choices. By the time Sunday rolls around, you only have 1 shirt left. You have no choice on Sunday—your decision was perfectly determined by the previous 6 days. You had 6 days of true flexibility, meaning your degrees of freedom are 6.

title: ST311 Review
text:
Degrees of freedom
Note: We need degrees of freedom because in a single mean test, we also have to use data to estimate \(s\) for the standard error. In a single proportion test, the standard error is entirely estimated using our statistic \(\hat{p}\). We will re-visit this when we review single proportion.
How many independent pieces of information you have
If you have \(\bar{x}\) and n = 50…. the 50th observation is “locked” into whatever the exact number makes the mean equal to \(\bar{x}\) (2035).
We are working with 49 degrees of freedom!
\(t_{49}\)

title: ST311 Review

Because our statistic follows a \(t_{49}\), it is essentially the same shape as a normal distribution. Because our test statistic is < 2, our p-value is going to be relatively large. Let’s calculate it.

Bayes’ Rule:
Everything we learn in ST-312 is from a frequentist perspective.
Bayes’ Rule has created a new way to think about statistics by showing how we can update our beliefs when new evidence becomes available. Instead of relying only on past data, Bayesian statistics combines prior knowledge with new evidence to make more informed conclusions.
\(\text{Posterior} = \frac{\text{Evidence} \times \text{Likelihood}}{\text{Prior}}\)
\(P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(B \mid A)P(A)}{P(B)}\)

title: Probability
text:
More practice
A company has two types of employees: 60% are experienced and 40% are new. An experienced employee has a 90% chance of completing a project on time, while a new employee has a 60% chance.
You randomly select an employee who completed their project on time. What is the probability that the employee is experienced?
What do we know? And what do we need to find out?

title: Probability
text:
What we know
\(P(E)=0.60\)
\(P(E^c)=0.40\)
\(P(O\mid E)=0.90\)
\(P(O\mid E^c)=0.60\)
What are we trying to solve?

title: Probability
text:
What we want
\(P(E\mid O)\)
We want to find the probability that the employee is experienced given that they completed the project on time.
So what else do we need?

title: Probability
text:
What we need
We need to find:
\(P(O)\)
Then we can use Bayes’ Rule:
\(P(E\mid O)=\frac{P(O\mid E)P(E)}{P(O)}\)
How do we find \(P(O)\)?

title: Probability
text:
P(O)
If I want the probability of O, I want the probability when O and E occur, and the probability when O and \(E^c\) occur….
Let’s think back to this rule: P(A|B) = \(\frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}\)
P(O|E) = \(\frac{P(O \cap E)}{P(E)}\)
How can we rewrite this?

title: Probability
text:
P(O)
\(P(O | E) = \frac{P(O \cap E)}{P(E)}\)
\(P(O\cap E)=P(O\mid E)P(E)\)
and
\(P(O| E^c) = \frac{P(O \cap E^c)}{P(E^c)}\)
\(P(O\cap E^c)=P(O\mid E^c)P(E^c)\)
and we should add them together to get \(P(O)\)!

Independence
Events are independent if the outcome of one event is not affected by the outcome of the other
We go from: \(P(A \cap B)\) = P(A|B)*P(B)
To: \(P(A \cap B)\) = P(A) * P(B)
